# claude-bughunter

> A self-contained Claude skill bundle for bug hunting and external red-team work · **84 skills** · 15 slash commands · **681 disclosed-report patterns** (433 now individually cited & auditable) across 24 core vulnerability classes · enterprise identity + infrastructure attack matrices · engagement-folder scaffolding · Burp MCP integration · battle-tested across authorized red-team and bug-hunting engagements, plus public training platforms (DVWA, OWASP Juice Shop, Hacker101, testphp.vulnweb.com).

Built by **Sachin Sharma** — Bug Hunting & GenAI Security Research.

 
   SPONSORED BY 
   
   
   
     
       
       
     
   
        
   
     
       
       
     
   
 

---

## What is this?

`claude-bughunter` is a drop-in skill bundle for the Claude Code skills system. Install once and Claude Code stops being a chatbot and starts behaving like a senior bug-hunting researcher or red-team operator: it knows the techniques, the chain templates, the VRT mappings, the platform CVE chains, and the hygiene — and it stays in scope.

Four layers stack:

- **Think** — `bb-methodology` + `redteam-mindset`: the 5-phase non-linear workflow, critical-thinking framework, and red-team operator discipline.
- **Hunt webapps** — 58 `hunt-*` skills curated from 681 disclosed HackerOne reports: per-class detection patterns, payloads, bypass tables, and chain templates.
- **Hit the perimeter** — enterprise platform chains (M365/Entra, Okta, vCenter, SSL-VPN appliances, SharePoint, cloud IAM): current 2024–2026 CVE chains + post-credential escalation.
- **Ship it** — `triage-validation` + reporting + `evidence-hygiene`: the 7-Question Gate, VRT-aware severity, OOS rebuttals, PII redaction, and red-team deliverables.

All triggered automatically by topic — describe what you're testing in plain English and the relevant skill loads. No invocation by name.

---

## Quickstart

**Option A — install as a Claude Code plugin (recommended).** From inside Claude Code:

```text
/plugin marketplace add elementalsouls/Claude-BugHunter
/plugin install claude-bughunter@elementalsouls
```

All 84 skills + 15 commands load namespaced under `claude-bughunter:` and update when you bump the plugin version — no files copied into `~/.claude/`.

**A HackerOne account is optional.** The install asks for a HackerOne API username and token. They only let the HackerOne MCP read your private programs and your own reports; leave both blank if you don't need that. Every skill, command and the MCP's public tools (duplicate search, program scope) work without them.

git clone https://github.com/elementalsouls/Claude-BugHunter.git
cd Claude-BugHunter
```

# macOS / Linux
bash scripts/install.sh

# Windows (PowerShell)
pwsh ./scripts/install.ps1
```

Superpowers is a complete software development methodology for your coding agents, built on top of a set of composable skills and some initial instructions that make sure your agent uses them.

## How it works

It starts from the moment you fire up your coding agent. As soon as it sees that you're building something, it *doesn't* just jump into trying to write code. Instead, it steps back and asks you what you're really trying to do. 

Once it's teased a spec out of the conversation, it shows it to you in chunks short enough to actually read and digest. 

After you've signed off on the design, your agent puts together an implementation plan that's clear enough for an enthusiastic junior engineer with poor taste, no judgement, no project context, and an aversion to testing to follow. It emphasizes true red/green TDD, YAGNI (You Aren't Gonna Need It), and DRY. 

Next up, once you say "go", it launches a *subagent-driven-development* process, having agents work through each engineering task, inspecting and reviewing their work, and continuing forward. It's not uncommon for your agent to work autonomously for a couple hours at a time without deviating from the plan you put together.

There's a bunch more to it, but that's the core of the system. And because the skills trigger automatically, you don't need to do anything special. Your coding agent just has Superpowers.

   "大道至简" 
 

 

中文 | English

 

* 此开源项目旨在完全从 0 开始，仅用 3 块钱成本与 2 小时训练时间，即可训练出规模约为 64M 的超小语言模型 MiniMind。
* MiniMind 系列极其轻量，主线最小版本体积约为 GPT-3 的 $\frac{1}{2700}$，力求让普通个人 GPU 也能快速完成训练与复现。
* 项目同时开源了大模型的极简结构与完整训练链路，覆盖 MoE、数据清洗、预训练（Pretrain）、监督微调（SFT）、LoRA、RLHF（DPO）、RLAIF（PPO / GRPO / CISPO）、Tool Use、Agentic RL、自适应思考与模型蒸馏等全过程代码。
* MiniMind 同时拓展了视觉模态模型 MiniMind-V、多模态 Omni 模型 MiniMind-O、扩散语言模型（MiniMind-dLM）、线性模型（MiniMind-Linear），详见 Discussion。
* 项目所有核心算法代码均从 0 使用 PyTorch 原生实现，不依赖第三方库提供的高层抽象接口。
* 这不仅是一个大语言模型全阶段开源复现项目，也是一套面向 LLM 入门与实践的教程。
* 希望此项目能为更多人提供一个可复现、可理解、可扩展的起点，一起感受创造的乐趣，并推动更广泛 AI 社区的进步。

> 注：本项目基于 Apache 2.0 协议开源，完全免费。“2 小时” 指 SFT 阶段在单张 NVIDIA 3090 上跑完 `1 epoch` 的实测耗时，“3 块钱” 指对应时段的 GPU 租用成本。

# 📌 项目介绍

大语言模型（Large Language Model, LLM）的出现，引发了全球范围内对 AI 的空前关注。无论是 ChatGPT、DeepSeek 还是 Qwen，都以惊艳的效果让人真切感受到这场技术浪潮的冲击力。然而，动辄数百亿参数的模型规模，使得它们对个人设备而言不仅难以训练，甚至连部署都显得遥不可及。打开大模型的“黑盒子”，真正去理解其内部运作机制，本应是一件令人心潮澎湃的事。遗憾的是，绝大多数探索最终都止步于使用 LoRA 等技术对现有大模型做少量微调，学习一些新指令或特定任务。这更像是在教牛顿如何使用 21 世纪的智能手机——虽然有趣，却偏离了理解物理本质的初衷。

与此同时，第三方的大模型框架与工具库，如 `transformers` / `trl` / `peft` 等，往往只暴露出高度抽象的接口。只需短短十几行代码，就可以完成“加载模型 + 加载数据集 + 推理 + 强化学习”的全流程训练。这种高效封装固然便利，却也在一定程度上把开发者与底层实现隔离开来，削弱了深入理解 LLM 核心代码的机会。我认为 “用乐高自己拼出一架飞机，远比坐在头等舱里飞行更让人兴奋”，然而更现实的问题是，互联网上充斥着大量付费课程和营销内容，用漏洞百出、一知半解的讲解包装所谓的 AI 教程。正因如此，本项目的初衷就是尽可能降低 LLM 的学习门槛，让每个人都能从理解每一行代码开始，从 0 开始亲手训练一个极小的语言模型。是的，从**零开始训练**，而不是仅仅停留在**推理**层面。最低只需不到 3 块钱的服务器成本，就能亲身体验从 0 到 1 构建一个语言模型的全过程。

😊 一起感受创造的乐趣吧！

- 提供 Tokenizer 与分词器训练代码，支持 ` `、` `、` ` 等模板标记。

- 提供全阶段开源数据，覆盖收集、蒸馏、清洗与去重后的高质量数据集。
- 关键训练算法与核心模块均从 0 实现，不依赖第三方框架封装。
- 兼容 `transformers`、`trl`、`peft` 等主流框架，以及 `llama.cpp`、`vllm`、`ollama` 等常用推理引擎与 `Llama-Factory` 等训练框架。
- 支持单机单卡与单机多卡（DDP、DeepSpeed）训练，支持 wandb / swanlab 可视化与动态启停训练。
- 支持在 C-Eval、C-MMLU、OpenBookQA 等第三方测评集上进行评测，并支持通过 YaRN 实现 RoPE 长文本外推。

# **🔥 Firecrawl**

**Knowledge infrastructure to make your agents smarter. 🔥** You can use Firecrawl three ways. This repo holds the code for Firecrawl Local and the self-hosted server, along with SDKs that work with all three.

- **Firecrawl Local.** Run Firecrawl on your own machine as one binary that turns websites into clean markdown, plugs into your AI agent as an MCP server and serves the Firecrawl API on localhost.
- **Firecrawl Cloud.** Use the hosted service at firecrawl.dev for everything Local does at scale with nothing to run, plus search and the 550+ data providers in Firecrawl Alexandria for far more knowledge than scraping alone.
- **Self-hosting.** Deploy the full Firecrawl server from `apps/api` with its own queues, workers and databases on your own infrastructure.

_Pst. Hey, you, join our stargazers :)_

 
   
 

---

## Firecrawl Local

Firecrawl Local scrapes, crawls and maps from your own machine without a database, queue or container, and it reaches Firecrawl Cloud when your AI agents need search or Alexandria. It installs from crates.io. You need Rust and a C compiler, which on macOS means `xcode-select --install` and on Debian or Ubuntu means `build-essential`.

```bash
cargo install firecrawl-local
```

If you don't have Rust, Firecrawl Cloud runs the same scrape with nothing to build and no signup.

```bash
npx -y firecrawl-cli@latest scrape https://firecrawl.dev
```

Scrape a page and print its markdown.

```bash
firecrawl-local scrape https://firecrawl.dev --markdown
```

Crawl a site and save one markdown file per page.

```bash
firecrawl-local crawl https://docs.firecrawl.dev --limit 50 --out ./pages
```

List every URL on a site.

```bash
firecrawl-local map https://firecrawl.dev
```

Pages that need JavaScript render in the Chrome or Chromium already on your machine, and PDFs and Office documents are parsed locally too. Without a browser, static pages still work and a page that needed one comes back with a warning.

### Add it to your AI agent

`init` finds Claude Code, Claude Desktop, Cursor, Windsurf, Gemini CLI and Codex on your machine and adds Firecrawl Local to each one as an MCP server. It backs up every config file first, and the MCP server itself needs Node.js 22 or newer.

```bash
firecrawl-local init
```

Restart your AI tool afterwards. Its scrape, crawl, map and batch scrape tools run on your machine, and the other Firecrawl tools go to Firecrawl Cloud.

### Run the Firecrawl API on localhost

`serve` answers the Firecrawl v2 API on port 3002, so code written for Firecrawl runs against it unchanged and local routes need no API key.

```bash
firecrawl-local serve
```

NGINX (pronounced "engine x" or "en-jin-eks") is the world's most popular Web Server, high performance Load Balancer, Reverse Proxy, API Gateway and Content Cache.

NGINX is free and open source software, distributed under the terms of a simplified 2-clause BSD-like license.

Enterprise distributions, commercial support and training are available from F5, Inc.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> The goal of this README is to provide a basic, structured introduction to NGINX for novice users. Please refer to the full NGINX documentation for detailed information on installing, building, configuring, debugging, and more. These documentation pages also contain a more detailed Beginners Guide, How-Tos, Development guide, and a complete module and directive reference.

NGINX is installed software with binary packages available for all major operating systems and Linux distributions. See Tested OS and Platforms for a full list of compatible systems.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> While nearly all popular Linux-based operating systems are distributed with a community version of nginx, we highly advise installation and usage of official packages or sources from this repository. Doing so ensures that you're using the most recent release or source code, including the latest feature-set, fixes and security patches.

## Modules
NGINX is comprised of individual modules, each extending core functionality by providing additional, configurable features. See "Modules reference" at the bottom of nginx documentation for a complete list of official modules.

NGINX modules can be built and distributed as static or dynamic modules. Static modules are defined at build-time, compiled, and distributed in the resulting binaries. See Dynamic Modules for more information on how they work, as well as, how to obtain, install, and configure them.

```bash
nginx -V

items.summary: OpenVINO™ is an open source toolkit for optimizing and deploying AI inference
items.content:
Open-source software toolkit for optimizing and deploying deep learning models.
 

 
   Documentation   •   Blog   •   Key Features   •   Tutorials   •   Integrations   •   Benchmarks   •   Generative AI  
 

[](https://badge.fury.io/py/openvino)
[](https://www.npmjs.com/package/openvino-node)
[](https://anaconda.org/conda-forge/openvino)
[](https://formulae.brew.sh/formula/openvino)

[](https://pepy.tech/project/openvino)
[](https://anaconda.org/conda-forge/openvino/files)
[](https://formulae.brew.sh/formula/openvino)
  

- **Inference Optimization**: Boost deep learning performance in computer vision, automatic speech recognition, generative AI, natural language processing with large and small language models, and many other common tasks.
- **Flexible Model Support**: Use models trained with popular frameworks such as PyTorch, TensorFlow, ONNX, Keras, PaddlePaddle, and JAX/Flax. Directly integrate models built with transformers and diffusers from the Hugging Face Hub using Optimum Intel. Convert and deploy models without original frameworks.
- **Broad Platform Compatibility**: Reduce resource demands and efficiently deploy on a range of platforms from edge to cloud. OpenVINO™ supports inference on CPU (x86, ARM), GPU (Intel integrated & discrete GPU) and AI accelerators (Intel NPU).
- **Community and Ecosystem**: Join an active community contributing to the enhancement of deep learning performance across various domains.

Check out the OpenVINO Cheat Sheet and Key Features for a quick reference.

## Installation

Get your preferred distribution of OpenVINO or use this command for quick installation:

```sh
pip install -U openvino
```

### Verify Installation

After installation, you can verify OpenVINO is installed correctly by running:

```python
import openvino as ov
print(ov.__version__)
```

Check system requirements and supported devices for detailed information.

## Tutorials and Examples

OpenVINO Quickstart example will walk you through the basics of deploying your first model.

Learn how to optimize and deploy popular models with the OpenVINO Notebooks 📚:
- Create an LLM-powered Chatbot using OpenVINO
- YOLOv11 Optimization
- Text-to-Image Generation
- Multimodal assistant with LLaVa and OpenVINO
- Automatic speech recognition using Whisper and OpenVINO

Discover more examples in the OpenVINO Samples (Python & C++) and Notebooks (Python).

Here are easy-to-follow code examples demonstrating how to run PyTorch and TensorFlow model inference using OpenVINO:

**PyTorch Model**

```python
import openvino as ov
import torch
import torchvision

# load PyTorch model into memory
model = torch.hub.load("pytorch/vision", "shufflenet_v2_x1_0", weights="DEFAULT")

# convert the model into OpenVINO model
example = torch.randn(1, 3, 224, 224)
ov_model = ov.convert_model(model, example_input=(example,))

# compile the model for CPU device
core = ov.Core()
compiled_model = core.compile_model(ov_model, 'CPU')

# infer the model on random data

**坐标：** 青岛下面非主城区
 
小区楼下有家理发店，之前原价 38，可以办 100 块钱三次的卡，已经觉得挺贵的了

这个**工资**不断**下跌**的时代，理发涨得这么快这么多真的正常吗 

我不理解这个世界了

items.title: 请问大家追求的是什么样的生活呢？
items.summary:
我今天在网上看到一篇纪念数学家、哲学家王浩的文章，里头提到哲学家何兆武。何兆武在他的《上学记》里谈到，有一次他和王浩讨论幸福问题，王浩最终同意了如下说法：幸福是日高日远的觉悟，是不断的拷问和扬弃，是通过苦恼的欢欣，而不是简单的信仰。

我觉得这句话就像阳光一样，一下子照亮我的内心了。只是叹息光阴似箭，年少时并不懂得珍惜。不知道大家都追求的是什么样的生活呢？大概正是人人都有不同的追求，这个世界才如此五彩缤纷吧。

items.summary:
大家好，虽说 23 年就注册了，但是也一直在潜水，第一条发帖就是索取求助，实在有些惭愧 🙏🏻，如果有说的不对的地方请多包涵。
### [我的背景]
- **学历**：民办二本，计算机科学与技术专业，27 届。
- **技术栈**：大三紧急突击了前端基础和框架，以及 Agent 相关内容（低代码、langchainrag 啥的）。
- **现状**：目前秋招颗粒无收，开发岗连实习都投不出结果，简历石沉大海。目前已经对写代码不感兴趣了。
### [困境与迷茫]
开发走不通后，我也在探索其他出路。之前了解过实施和售前，但我越看越迷茫：
1. **岗位体验存疑**：了解了一下发现“售前”非常偏商务和讲 PPT，对 i 人很不友好；而“实施”好像偏向现场部署和维护，似乎沟通压力小一些？不知道真实的工作日常是怎样的。
2. **技能要求抽象**：就比如售前要求“商业思维”、“懂行业痛点”，作为还没毕业的应届生，完全不知道怎么去培养或在简历上体现。
3. **底线**：暑假干过流水线两班倒赚钱和外卖，实在不想干这些血汗活了，想找个正经工作。
### [真心求教]
想请教一下各位前辈大佬，像我这种“民办二本 + 无技术大厂实习 + i 人”应届生：
- **除开发外，还有哪些对 i 人相对友好、门槛没那么高的 IT 岗位？**（比如测试、技术支持、数据运维、产品运营等，哪个方向目前对应届生相对机会多一点？）
- **“实施工程师”或“技术支持”的真实体验如何？** 有没有这两类岗位的前辈能分享一下日常工作内容和职业发展路径？
- **如果现在开始转向，我该重点补充什么技能或准备什么样的小项目？**
- **除了计算机还有什么行业推荐？**

非常害怕毕业即失业，感谢每一个愿意回帖指点的大佬，祝大家工作顺利，代码无 BUG！

items.content: Commitment issues (app edition) - by Ben Tossell Ben’s Bites Subscribe Sign in Commitment issues (app edition) It’s not me, it’s you Ben Tossell Nov 24, 2026 52 1 Share Last week, a mathematician spent six weeks with Claude and proved the Riemann hypothesis. A maths problem nobody had cracked since 1859. Then there’s me. I built a clock. P.s. The full interactive version of this post is here . Something in my tiny pea brain stops me working out What time is 10am PT in UK? without using super intelligence. I’m not proud of my chat history. It’s as bad as my calculator history. 200+65 is 265 btw. My clock lives in my menu bar. Type a time and a city, or drag it, and every city changes. presets for demo only It handles daylight savings too. Because of course the UK and US change their clocks on different weekends. You may be thinking ‘There’s a million clock apps that do this for free’. And you’re absolutely right. But I’ve got commitment issues. I’m always window shopping. Lots of apps are good enough but it feels like the grass is always greener. A lot of great tools come down to a few small features I really like. But they’re not making it for me. They’re making it for everyone. They need more users, so they add more features, and they put the price up. Or they’re free and get forgotten. It’s not me, it’s you. And I’m no better with AI models. Right now I’m using Gemini 4 Neon after turning my back on Google. A new model comes around and I pack my bags and move in. I obviously need the best to answer my very hard questions. The trouble with juggling multiple models at once is keeping track of them. Who am I neglecting? Who’s about to cut me off? Other apps I tried had more than I needed, so I made a stripped down version with just the things I care about. sliding usage is just used to show the menu icon syncing Screenshots are another one. I take a lot of full-page screenshots. Things I’ve built, to check them, or sites I like the look of, to ‘borrow’ from. So now I have an extension that does that. Browsers are a different beast. They’re a marriage. We spend a lot of time in them. So this relationship has been one of my biggest headaches. I’m sure I could build my own but it feels like a lot of work. I loved Arc, like many others. Then they got bought and ditched it. So I went back to Chrome. Then the people behind Arc came out with Dia, so I went crawling back to my ex, who’d had some work done. It was kinda the same but not quite. Then I dated someone literally named after both of my exes, Arc and Dia - Ardia. No red flags there. Then it got slow. So I stopped looking and just taught Chrome all my ex’s best moves: A way to ‘peek’ links - which shows you a mini window of the page you click Click to open a page in split view Vertical tabs (Chrome added this anyway) Ad blocking, no cookie banners And my biggest need - the tab switcher. I built my own extension + mac app that does all of that. Plus I can add in some extra niceties like defaulting

And it’s a remote company spread across every time zone, so someone is always awake. The average ChatGPT user sends about 4 messages a day, and a reply is roughly 500 words now. With over a billion people using the big AI chatbots, that’s about 6 billion messages every day. 10.4 million people typing at world-record speed, round the clock, with no sleep, no lunch, and no days off. Okay, let’s run it like a real company instead. Which means it needs a CEO. Me. 11.8 billion internal messages a day, just to keep the place running. Oh, and we still have to answer the 6 billion messages people actually sent us. All in, you’d need 77.4 million staff just to keep 10.4 million people typing at any given moment. If you want to check my maths: a 40-hour week, time off from a 2025 survey of UK call centres , 12.1 people per manager ( the US average ), and 2 HR people per 100 staff ( SHRM ). People quit at the US rate , earn the US median for customer service , and get 153 chat messages a day , like the average Microsoft Teams user. The biggest Zoom call holds 1 million . Giving machines more to read barely helped, because they could only see the last couple of words. Try guessing what comes after “speak fluent…” with no other clues. In 2017, eight people at Google let it see every word at once and weigh the ones that matter, like France. They called that attention, and the machine a transformer. It’s the T in ChatGPT. Suddenly, giving it more to read actually worked. More text, bigger brain, better guesses. Writing a reply is the same thing. items.content: Productiv-icky - by Ben Tossell - Ben's Bites Ben’s Bites Subscribe Sign in Productiv-icky Digging holes on the beach Ben Tossell Nov 17, 2026 79 4 2 Share productiv-icky (adj.) - the feeling of doing work you didn’t mean to do We have a problem. full interactive post is here We agree this is insane, right? Someone I don’t know sends me emails that I’m expected to reply to. I don’t know them. I don’t work for them. So I ignore them (well actually I send them to email jail). Nuh-uh, that’s not my work, buddy. But it’s different if it’s my super-intelligent, helpful agent friend… Yeses are easy. They’re quick. But every yes has a yes-tax. The hidden extra work you didn’t think of. The long tail of regret where you question why you ever said yes. Say I did reply to those emails, they’d send me stuff to read to show how great they are at their job and how much better I’d be. Then we’d organise a call (which would derail whichever day that call was on). Then we’d have follow-up items. Then a string of other crap I couldn’t care less about. I know what’s going to happen. I can smell it, it stinks. I’ve said yes and paid the tax many times before. Now I pay $200/mo for a super-intelligent, over-eager, needy little nerd to ping me incessantly about taking things off my plate. I feel bad for him. He wants to work. He’s gagging for it. Just. One. More. Task. Master. Plus, my little nerd has a gambling problem. Or rather, he feeds mine. Remember years ago sending tons of Slack messages to get the most out of your $20/mo plan? Nor me. Why? Because it’s dumb. But now we feel like we should use all our tokens before they run out. Why? Because everyone else is. We started measuring shovels instead of the hole. Someone’s needy little nerd booked their dentist, replied to their mum and launched a business whilst they were asleep. They’ve got an org chart. For nerds. With a Chief of Staff. You feel behind. Like way behind. So you grab a shovel and start digging. A little hole over there to triage your inbox, one here to draft your tweets, one to check on those. Then you spend your day checking the holes are being dug right. Before long, you’re surrounded by holes and a mountain of dirt you gotta do something with. Now as a man, holes are hardwired into my DNA. A few beers, a beach and a shovel, I’m digging a hole. I’d take pride in it. I’d make the best one, impressively round, deep enough to see sea water seep through the bottom. But I’d only dig one. There’s a whole beach but I chose this spot. Next time the needy little nerd pings you: do you really want another hole? Also, don’t dig big holes on the beach. They collapse. If you haven’t read it, you can get a copy here . I have had the chance to use the new Claude Fable 5.2 quite a bit before its public launch 1 , and it is very impressive, following on the already excellent Opus 5.5. AI has gotten so good, in fact, that it is worth asking if Anthropic’s newest models (and the inevitable competing models OpenAI and Google will soon release) cross the boundary into being an Artificial General Intelligence? AGI is a much-debated term with a lot of potential definitions. For this post, I’ll go with: “an AI as good as most human experts at most intellectual tasks you can do with a computer.” This explicitly excludes a lot of human work, including interacting with the physical world and other people, as well as most actual jobs, where “using a computer” is just one task among many. Still, even with these caveats, building a limited form of AGI has long been the goal of AI developers. So as not to keep you in suspense, I think the answer is that this is “almost” AGI, or what I have called Jagged AGI. Even within my limited definition, there are still important areas in many tasks where AI is jagged enough to fall well behind human capability. But the jaggedness is no longer about simple errors or hallucinations, which makes it harder to describe. So I want to try to do that in this post by showing you what Fable can do and where the gaps are. To get started I asked the new model: “I write OneUsefulThing among other stuff, I need you to create the most impressive thing I can share with people when you launch. It needs to be embeddable in a post and i can preface it however you like. it needs to have a visceral impact on people to show what you can do and the range of capabilities. It should grab them quickly. Be amazingly clever about this.” Fable asked me not to reveal anything until you had watched its video to the end. This was in one shot, with no feedback from me beyond the prompt. There is creativity here (including in the twist ending) and judgment and playfulness and cleverness. This is, I think, at the level of a human expert trying to make a movie with code alone, the sort of performance I would once have associated with AGI. The “G” in AGI Code and video creation have been areas where AI development has focused, so is Fable 5.2 really a General Intelligence? Looking back across the gap between these books is a good way to get a sense of AI progress. And, thanks to AI, I can describe this progress with some quite lovely charts. Making the charts is itself a good indicator of how far things have come. In the era of chatbots, the era of Co-Intelligence , I would have had to work back-and-forth with an AI in a chat window, guiding it through each new step. In the current era of agentic AI that I cover in Co-Existence , I delegated the work and let the AI handle it. In this case, I used Opus 5.5 in Claude Projects, which allows you to talk to a single “orchestrator” agent that then spins off additional agents as needed, giving them instructions and relaying information back to you. Getting the work done was straightforward. I gave the AI a couple sentences of suggestions and it did what would have taken me hours of work (all the research, all the graphing, all the layouts, all the images, all the citations…) in minutes. And since I didn’t have to do the work, I had the AI make many options for me. I picked some and gave handwavy reactions to others that would drive a human team mad (“make it better”). items.content: The Dot and the Swarm - by Ethan Mollick - One Useful Thing One Useful Thing Subscribe Sign in The Dot and the Swarm Benefitting from the Bitter Lesson Ethan Mollick Oct 01, 2026 1,409 236 144 Share I generally think I have done a good job anticipating the direction and pace of AI over the few years I have been writing this Substack, but I think I recently got something fairly large wrong. In the last year I have been posting about how I suspected that humans would have to approach working with agents as a manager, deciding how to delegate work to agents and specifying how those agents should be organized. I thought that getting agents to work effectively as a group would take careful construction, akin to building a company, and that this would take time to figure out. Nope. I fell prey to The Bitter Lesson, the hard truth, learned over and over again, that things that we thought required elaborate human rules and thinking can be solved with the brute force of better machine learning systems and more AI. The Bitter Lesson is everywhere among AI startups and companies adopting AI. A huge amount of effort went into building elaborate computer systems to feed AIs the right information at the right time, but AI systems have learned to seek out information themselves. The same thing happened to prompting. People built elaborate templates and chains of prompts that walked the AI through a task one step at a time. Then newer models turned out to be better at planning the steps themselves, and, as our research shows , planning steps have much less value. The history of the Bitter Le— — you know what? I don’t really need to explain the Bitter Lesson, I asked Claude to do it in a music video. With one prompt, Fable wrote the lyrics and submitted it to Suno; Opus 5.5 did everything else using code alone without any image generation (How did Opus 5.5 pull this off? The Bitter Lesson tells you!). I gave no feedback at all. As somebody who teaches managers and has published research on management, I guess I believed that managing agents would be different. Humans have been working on management for a very long time without fully figuring it out. It seemed like the kind of thing that would need to be designed by people, at least for a while. It turns out that organizing work is just one more thing AI can learn to do. Which brings us to dots and Muse. Nathan Lambert Nov 14, 2026 127 24 21 Share Article voiceover 0:00 -7:28 Audio playback is not supported on your browser. Please upgrade. The resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is a major setback for the US development of an open model ecosystem. Nvidia still has the financial interests in supporting open models, which are to avoid concentration in power among a few customers who would develop their own chips and reduce Nvidia’s profits, but supporting the open ecosystem is a tricky puzzle more than an engineering problem to grind out a solution on. Nvidia’s business operations are famously extremely dependent on Jensen as an operator, so it is a consensus opinion that there are challenges ahead (or even more high-profile departures through chip-smuggling investigations or plain-old sharks circling more poachable talent). Nvidia’s number one goal is to stabilize the ship, deliver to customers in the next 24 months, and prevent implosion. Open models have been one of Jensen’s more ambitious, founder-style bets. He has been flooding the zone with funding in a way that will very likely dry up. Interconnects AI is a reader-supported publication. To receive new posts and support my work, consider becoming a free or paid subscriber. Subscribe In this period, the open model economy is in its nascency. These are crucial years for establishing use-cases, revenue flow, and motives to continue training the next generation models. I discussed the sensitivity of these early years in my recent talk at Fireworks Forge ( slides , recording ). The core of the argument is one upside for open models, a reason to be optimistic, and one downside. The positive case is that the open model economy has correctly latched onto “ownership of intelligence” and enterprise post-training as a crucial lane. What is to be determined is exactly how big the downstream market is. The downside is that the true long-term benefit of open models, as truly commoditized intelligence, is very far from realization with compute in such short supply. In the near term, where inference startups are also struggling to get enough chips (because Anthropic and OpenAI are buying so much capacity), there’s little margin competition on open-weight models. If open-source models are also served at giant inference margins, as we learned with DeepSeek’s DeepInfer release, they’re far from a commodity. In this paradigm, the closed labs with better economies of scale and integration from model to datacenter and chips will win. I expanded on this challenge in my recent piece on the open model economy . Together, a lot still needs to go right for open models to be a meaningful economic engine.
